I've run 20,000 ads and spent $150M on Meta . Benchmarks I've found over 6 years: 1. 1 new creative concept per $10k in monthly spend. At $500k/month that's 50 concepts (~3 ads per concept, more for static-heavy). 2. At $100k/mo, aim for 70% new concepts and 30% variations. As you scale past $1m/mo, max out at 50/50. But never drop below 50% new. 3. 70% of your creatives should be cut before week 2. Only 10-20% will ever hit your performance threshold. If you're keeping most of your ads alive, you're probably losing money. 4. Your top 1-2% of ads should drive 50% of total spend. If they don't, you haven't found real winners yet or you haven't utilized them well enough. 5. Big swings have lower hit rates (5-10%) but higher total potential. These are the ads that can scale to $1m+ in spend. 6. 70% video, 30% static for most ecom brands. New brands need more video (more education, less BOF audience). Clothing should lean heavier static (lots of SKUs to show). 7. 15-20% of budget goes to testing. Under 10% and your creative pipeline dries up. Over 25% and you're burning cash without enough scale behind winners. 8. When you 2x spend, expect 20-30% ROAS decline. A $30 CPA at $50k/month might become $40 at $200k. Scale requires better ads, better optimization, better structure, or lower targets. 9. Limit bid and budget changes to 25% max. For 90% of changes, smaller and more frequent changes outperform bigger ones. 10. Meta always targets returning customers. Aim to keep returning conversions under 15-20%. Accept it and plan around it. 11. Ad copy can improve performance up to 50%. But a great ad outperforms by 500%. Copy matters, but the creative itself is where the real leverage is. 12. A great media buyer improves ROAS 100%+ vs a bad one. Creative strategists make better decisions when they're working off clean data and with better media buyers, because the scaled ads are actual winners. Hope this helps. What others have I missed?

I spoke to a Sales leader this week. She joined a new company 2 months ago. She's meeting with their existing vendors to evaluate which contracts she'll renew, which ones she'll expand, and which ones she'll cancel. She had 3 renewal convos this week. Guess how many of those convos left her wanting to renew or expand? 0. She works for a large company. Two are 6-figure contracts, one is 5-figures. They're well-known, "AI-pilled" vendors. You've see them on stages talking about how they've optimized their Sales orgs with AI. And, everyone sits in the audience ooh-ing and ahh-ing and thinking, "We better do this, too". And, yet, we don't stop and ask, "Do these tactics make the experience better for the buyer?". Call me a luddite (I've been called a lot worse), but I think the most important quality in a Sales leader operating in this "Look....a squirrel! Look...a squirrel!" AI era we're living is restraint. OpenClaw! Go buy Mac Minis! AI SDRs! Fire the SDRs! Agentforce! Automate everything! Muse! OMG have you tried it?! Instinct! It's changing the game! ChatGPT/Claude! Use it for everything! A Sales leader can't be the talking dog, Doug, from the movie Up. Yes, it's great to experiment. But, being AI-pilled doesn't equate to making the buyer experience better. And, every time you send a "we should be doing this, too" message to the team, you risk distracting them from what actually matters. How they're showing up in buyer interactions. One of the easiest ways to win right now is to outperform in the Sales conversation. Whether that's new logo, renewal, or expansion. Win on the ability to offer an experience that leaves the buyer thinking, "Wow, they came prepared. That was an insightful and useful conversation". Win on reducing their effort to make the case to renew you or buy you. Win on giving a shit about what their business is trying to achieve (vs. just pointing them PowerPoint slides, dashboards, and usage reports and telling a usage story). I'm all for AI that makes the buyer experience better. There are so many ways it can. But, FFS, you don't need to come home from a conference this week and implement every AI tactic you saw someone present on a stage. Buyer experience > everything.

LTV → Focus on the first 90 days. → Second-purchase offer timed to actual consumption. → Subscription onboarding that cuts cancel rate in month two. I've sold $450M of DTC products I see a NEW arbitrage for premium eCom: AppLovin Ads: → Placements inside mobile games and apps. → The ad takes the full screen. → Rewarded video: the user is locked in for 15-30 seconds to earn extra lives or in-game currency. → Interstitial: a 3-second unskippable window before the Skip button appears. A few years ago I would have laughed at putting a $60 physical product in the middle of someone's mobile game. Going into 2026 and 2027, these networks are performing well for premium eCom brands. (Especially those selling to 40 to 50 year old women.) But you need different creative for AppLovin: Rewarded video (locked in 15-30 seconds) → 0 to 25s: tell a story, show a satisfying demo, entertain them while they wait → 26 to 28s: build tension, this is the riser → 29 to 30s: strongest CTA, timed for the second before they can close it Interstitial (3-second window, then Skip appears) → Don't open on your hook. At second 0 they're annoyed and hunting for the X. → Reverse-engineer it. Seconds 0 to 3 build toward the hook. → The hook lands at second 3, the moment Skip becomes tappable. → This is the opposite of Meta where you're interrupting the scroll and trying to hook for the first 3 seconds. Cheatsheet: - Take your 3 best-performing Meta concepts - Recut the timing around the placement UI - Run rewarded and interstitial as separate tests - Judge the channel on blended MER, in-app attribution is messier than Meta's Anyone else testing AppLovin? Two-month sale → ~50% of revenue lands in November and December → 12% of it comes on Black Friday alone → $400 average order value, $699 for the 12-piece set 2. Consideration window → Under 20% of purchases happen inside a 7-day window → 80-85% of buyers say they knew HexClad for months first → Only ~26% of the country is ever "in market" for premium cookware 3. October loss → They run October MER 33% below their year-end target → The 13 days before the sale run about 50% below that → "That's going to allow us to spend into a full funnel" (Connor Rolain, Head of Growth) 4. Black Friday incrementality → ROAS lift peaks over 300% on Nov 12-13, before the sale opens → Black Friday weekend has the lowest lift of the whole period → Jason Panzer, President, left ~$1M of BFCM budget unspent: "It's bottom of funnel now. We did the work all throughout the year." 5. Forecast locked early → Offers, timing and targets set 15 weeks out → 85% of November revenue comes from the sale window → Set expectations to stay the course in October and build demand It's not easy to run marketing like HexClad. You need to have faith in your brand, and forecast incredibly well.

I've consulted founders doing $2M - $10M/year on their content strategy. They rarely have more than 10k followers. If you're confused over content strategy (+ want to build inbound) here's my advice: Stop over engineering your content into a funnel. TOFU MOFU BOFU. LinkedIn isn't a linear funnel where people find you, then trust you, then enquire with you all in one simple straight line. They might find you one day with a BOFU post, not a TOFU post. Then they might not see you again for another 2 months. And when they do, it's a TOFU post. Then they might go check out your profile. Then your website. Then sign up to your newsletter. Then they might read one or two of your emails. Then they might ignore your emails for another 3 months. Then they might see one of your MOFU posts on LinkedIn. See how this CAN go? There's no way you can really predict what a prospect will do. The only advice I can give you that is simple enough to not drive yourself insane is this: Marketing, specifically social content, is a long game of staying top of mind. People overcomplicate this waaayyy too much. Stay top of mind. That's it. Mix personal stories with proof and case studies, sure. Post consistently, sure. You don't know who's watching, where they're at, or what they need to see before they reach out. So just keep showing up as the obvious person for the thing you do. P.S. Are your new creatives actually diverse? How to tell: 1. Download every active ad including ad spend, headline, body, script, on-screen text 2. Transcribe every single ad with timestamps 3. AI tag every ad with format, angle, hook style, creator and core selling point 4. Vectorize every ad so it has a data point on an n-dimensional space 5. Flag the near-duplicates by measuring cosine similarity of >0.95 6. Cluster into concepts by grouping the vectors 7. Measure concentration with Herfindahl index (economists use this to measure market monopolies) If you have too much concentration your account is at risk from fatigue. One idea gets tired, and the whole account goes with it. Summary: - AI tag every ad you run for analysis - Vectorize and measure concentration to go deeper

Did the customer come from Google or Meta ? Better way to check: - Pull your post purchase survey responses - Look at answer: "Where did you first hear about us?" - Match each answer to the UTM on that same order. - Create a heatmap grid of where they found you vs UTM codes What you'll see: - Post purchase tends to report awareness channels (TikTok, Meta etc) - UTM tends to report demand capture channels (SEO, Google etc) - Using this you’ll spend less on Google, maybe more on Meta, and more on TikTok. How you use this data: → Use it to know which channels are driving awareness that converts → Push into those channels to grow the brand → Extrapolate the survey across all new customers and calculate cost per new customer per channel. Caveats: → Make sure you have 30%+ response rate before you analyze → Aim for 100+ responses minimum per channel row. And while you're in there, add some more post purchase questions in: "Why did you buy today?" = creative strategy "Anything you almost didn't buy over?" = objection handling "Any issues with the site?" = CRO roadmap "Anything you wish we sold?" = product development Hope this helps

Have an in-flight deal that's gone quiet on you? Stop making excuses for your prospect ("I'm sure they're just busy!"). When a deal goes quiet, job #1 is to get to the truth. Here are 3 messages I use to do that (+ when I'd use each one): 1. Unexpected Roadblock I use this when my gut is telling me that something went sideways and the prospect is hesitant to share bad news with me. Fun fact - the more pleasant/nice you are, the harder it often is for a prospect to tell you bad news. People don't like the way they feel about themselves when they tell someone who did their job well, "no". Make it easy for them. 2. The "New Idea" This is my go-to for deals that went quiet a couple quarters ago (works for closed-lost deals, too). It's a way to re-engage them that isn't "want to revisit buying our stuff?". And, it grounds the convo in something happening in their business. Good for when you know your deal isn't attached to anything urgent. 3. "Elephant in the Room" or "Rookie Mistake" I use this when I realize I got happy ears and rushed a deal. I label what I think I goofed and invite the prospect to correct me. This one is especially effective if you didn't help your prospect build the business case. So many deals get stuck here. The best sellers still have deal risk. They're just proactive about addressing the elephant in the room before the prospect does. Try one - and please do let me know if it works for you. I love seeing sellers win. Good luck!

Clay is ruining cold email. Take it from someone who spent 4 years sending 300+ outbound emails every single day. Outbound used to be about finding what resonated. You tested a core pain point, measured the response, and refined the message. Today, I watch outbound teams build massive Clay tables to hyper-personalize They scrape every detail they can find on a prospect, generate custom copy for every lead, and hit send. Then the campaign falls flat, and they have no idea why. Start with the offer. Then personalize. Here is the cold outbound testing hierarchy that books me consistent 3.7% positive replies: 1// Test the offer first Find an offer that pulls before writing custom copy. ↳ Keep copy standardized across the test cohort ↳ Zero deep personalization beyond basic account fields ↳ Test distinct value propositions against each other ↳ Run each offer until you establish a clean baseline Target: ~1% baseline positive reply rate on a standardized email. If an audience will not respond to the core offer with standard copy, personalizing the first sentence will not save it. Example: “Would you be interested if I built you a contact list of your past clients who just changed jobs and aren't working with you yet?” 2// Hyper-personalization testing Personalization does work, but it needs to be standardized and tested thoroughly. If you run offer testing against 100+ daily sends, pair it down to 10 per day. This will give you the ability to hyper-customize. ↳ Do a ton of research on the person, a little nugget about them and mention it to them in email, super casual.↳ Then find them on all social platforms possible (Instagram, LinkedIn, X, Facebook)↳ Message them on all those platforms to give you a higher probability of being seen.↳ This takes 10 outreaches per day and 3-4x’s it. ↳ Copy and paste the same message and say “btw I reached out to you via email also” This is how you hit 25% reply rate on a small list. Same impact as 100+ emails per day. 2// Personalization + Offer = Scale ↳ Keep the winning offer and call to action identical ↳ Your manual personalization work will help you ID the 2-3 types of customized messages that work. Wrap them around a specific pain or buying trigger (Clay is great for this part!) Target: scale reply rates up to 3-5%.With buying triggers I see positive replies above 6%. Testing constraints: 1 // Cohorts ↳ 1 industry ↳ 1 buyer committee role ↳ 300 contacts per test cohort ↳ 2 emails per contact 2 // Send limits ↳ Never hit the same contact with more than 1 offer per month ↳ Tag every record with the offer version and cohort outcome This testing system means: - You know exactly which offer generates pipeline - Personalization scales a working message instead of hiding a weak one This is the rigor that outbound teams need.

VP of Sales: "We're losing to competitors" So I read all 35,000 of their closed lost deals. Not one was tagged competitor. When a revenue number misses, the default suspects are always product, lead gen, or the competition. Then you open the CRM activity logs. On their largest deals, over 18 months: ↳ The median won deal took 13 contact attempts ↳ The median lost deal stopped at 5 ↳ The median disqualified deal stopped at 3 But here's the part that actually matters. With the same deals and size band, the only variable was who owned them: ↳ Top rep: 34% win rate ↳ Team average: 19% ↳ Shared inbound queue: 5% ↳ No owner assigned: 0% The deal didn't decide. The routing did. 55 of those deals were worth $694k combined and were never assigned to anyone. Median contact attempts: zero. They won none of them. And the ones that die don't get closed out. A deal they win closes in 36 days. A deal they lose sits open for 165 days before anyone marks it dead. So reps spend months staring at bloated pipeline, convincing themselves coverage is fine, working deals that died last quarter. Here's the fix: 1 // Fix routing before you fix reps ↳ Kill the shared inbound queue for anything above your ACV threshold & assign it to a human on arrival. ↳ Audit unowned pipeline weekly. Zero is the only acceptable number. ↳ Reassign books held by departed reps within 48 hours, not "eventually." 2 // Enforce persistence thresholds Deals we invested in closed at roughly 10x the rate of deals we didn't. Some of that is that good deals attract effort. Some of it isn't. ↳ Validation rules so opportunities can't be marked closed-lost below a minimum touch count. ↳ Multi-channel, not single-channel bursts. ↳ Track average contact attempts per opportunity by rep, and coach on the gap. 3 // Age out the rot When dead pipeline sits open for 165 days, forecast accuracy is fiction. ↳ Alert the moment a deal exceeds 2x average cycle time. ↳ Stage duration limits: advance it or disqualify it. ↳ Route abandoned accounts back to nurture instead of letting them decay in open pipeline. Don't let Meta pick your winning ads

Without doing this:

I recently ran an analysis for a brand with two products.

They were judging their ads on in-platform day-one or 7-day click CPA.

Product A
→ Converted great on day one
→ Tapered off fast after that
→ Lower AOV product
→ Easy decision for the consumer to buy

Product B
→ Looked worse on day-one and 7-day click
→ Longer consideration cycle, higher AOV
→ Ended up the best product after we waited 15+ days
→ Won by even more once we layered in incrementality

Follow Meta's in-platform metrics and we kill Product B. Meta was losing the conversion event proven by incrementality testing, and it is what we have been told to blindly trust.

But there is more to attribution than what Meta reports.

1. Compare 1, 7 and 28-day windows. (Start with in platform then move to incrementality testing)
→ That gap is your purchase velocity. Promos convert inside the 1-day window. Awareness ads show up at 28.
→ A high-AOV ad that looks dead at day 7 could still climbing at day 28.

2. Judge new-customer CPA in your MTA.
→ Triple Whale or Northbeam shows who bought and where they came from first.
→ Meta may miss the ad that opened the consideration cycle. And they report all customers not just new.

3. Give high-AOV ads 30 days before you cut.
→ Days 20-40 is where the repurchases land.
→ Cut at day 7 to look efficient and you never see them.

Day-one CPA tells you which ad converts fastest.
It tells you nothing about which one drives your LTV.

P.S. This isn’t sponsored but Churney has a cool free tool to see how much impact LTV has and if this should be a concern in your account. It isn’t always an issue. Just look up “churney growth predictability test”

How to manage cost/bid cap Meta campaigns

You need to stay right side of the slope:

You have two dials to achieve high scale and low CPA.
- Moving budget up or down
- Moving bid up or down

If you're under budget:
→ Want better performance? Bid down, budget down.
→ Want more scale? Bid up, budget the same.
→ Want to scale hard? Push both.

The moment you ARE hitting your budget, the bid is how you protect efficiency:
→ Performance just okay? Budget up, bid down.
→ Performance good? Budget up, leave the bid.
→ Performance strong? Budget up, bid up. Let it rip.

IM8 Health launched 10,000 ads since June.

Isn't that WAY too many???

→ Launched in June, already running 10,000 ads
→ A chunk of the output, in my opinion, is AI slop
→ Their last reported quarter put $22.2M of marketing against $23.3M of gross profit

So why 10,000 ads?

Heres my take:

1. Marketing eats gross profit

→ Q1 revenue $36M, gross profit $23.3M on a 65% margin
→ Selling and marketing came in at $22.2M, so 95% of gross profit went straight back out to acquisition
→ Loss from operations $8.9M, and adjusted EBITDA loss widened to $5.6M from $4.5M a year earlier
→ Net loss reads $23.1M, but $17.8M of that is non-cash marks on digital assets and warrants
→ Revenue grew 6x YoY and the cost base scaled right along with it

2. Orders went backwards

→ Q1 orders came in at 220,000, down from 230,000+ in Q4
→ Revenue climbed 23% QoQ anyway, on $240 new customer AOV and ~79% of new customers subscribing
→ So the growth came out of order value while the customer count fell

3. Someone else funds 70% of CAC

→ General Catalyst's $1B CVF finances up to 70% of IM8's customer acquisition cost
→ It books as a financial liability, repaid out of revenue from those customers
→ The return sits below operating income as interest expense, so it never touches gross margin
→ 100% of the marketing keeps landing in S&M, which is why that line looks so heavy

Payback is ~3.5 months and 70% of the CAC is financed.

Volume is the obvious lever to pull.

But this invites natural failure points
→ Too many low-quality ads
→ Too many ads carrying legal risk
→ Too many near-identical ads splitting the same audience
→ Brand consistency begins to slip

For one of our customers we're getting 80 to 100 positive responses a day and I don't touch the account. A Grok bot does four jobs on a cron.

Here's what has to stay true every day or a campaign like this dies.

1. Enough leads in the campaign.

Every day Grok Bot checks how many leads are not started. If it's ever under 100,000 it pulls from our Supabase, which tracks who we emailed in the last 60 days, who we re-reached in the last 30, and what month we last touched them, so nobody gets hit more than once a quarter. Then it fires them at a Clay webhook and the Clay CLI workflow does the cleanup, the enrichment, and the AI content.

2. Volume actually going out.

At noon it checks how many emails went out that day. If something locked up and we're under-sending, it rechecks the campaigns and refills them itself.

3. Daily Deliverability check

It reads our inbox table in Supabase every morning. If a domain was replying at 1.5% and drops to 0.2% day over day, it pulls that domain out, cancels the subscription, and swaps another one in.

4. The Friday inbox destroyer

Every Friday it looks for domains that have sent over 200 emails with under a 0.7% reply rate overall. Those get scheduled for cancellation and pulled out of the campaigns. Then it tells me how many domains we need to buy to replace them. I audit that, make the correction, and put the order in at Hypertide.

The reason it's Grok Bot and not the other agent harnesses is boring. The cron job actually fires. I have set one up in Hermes, then checked in three times wondering why it never ran. 

Codex or Claude schedules can totally do this too but if my computer is off it won't run.

Yesterday, I lost a 3000-person January SKO workshop deal. Here's exactly what I did to lose it (and how you can lose deals, too). 

First, am I bummed? Of course. It would've been an awesome logo. It had all the markings of a deal that should close. Former client introduced me. On a texting basis with the champion. Champion looped me in with her boss + peers for conversations. She, personally, wanted it to happen. Clear COI against a '27 CEO business objective. 

But, these are exactly the type of deals that used to stay in my pipeline for months. Because I didn't want to hear bad news. So, I didn't make it easy for prospects to give it to me. So, I'd stall until I got desperate for an answer at EOQ.  As a result, I'd leave myself no time to fill my pipeline gap. And, I'd frustrate my manager when my forecast would bottom out 2 days before EOQ. 

One of the great things about my business now is that I HAVE to be better at disqualifying. If I hold a January SKO date, and the customer gives me a no in November, it's unlikely I'll book another one for that day. 

So, here are the two things I did to lose the deal early (that any seller can copy): 

1. In the discovery call, I asked a direct question: "I hope I've earned the right for you to be transparent with me. What, in your opinion, are the most likely reasons your CRO would say no to our idea?". She gave me 2 reasons. 

2. When I didn't hear from her for a couple days, I sent her a text. "Hi! If you hit a sticking point, or heard bad news, you can tell me." Other times, I'll use "Did we hit an unexpected roadblock?". Or, "Did REASON end up happening?". 

The key is that YOU are the one to label the bad news. If you did #1 in discovery, you already know the likely deal threats. Be the one to throw one out in the open, first. If we're wrong, they'll correct us. 

This is especially true if you have good rapport with your prospect. In general, humans don't like the way they feel about themselves when they tell someone they like, "no". Be the one to put the bad news out there, first. 

I got a reply right away that reason #1 was it. "I've been holding out hope that we can keep pushing, but unfortunately.....". 

Of course, it's a bummer to lose a deal. But a GREAT seller has a 30% win rate. That means they lose 7 deals and win 3. 

We can't be afraid to hear bad news. It's part of the job. It's WHEN we hear the bad news that makes the difference. Your time is your most precious commodity.  

Lastly - I sent a note to the leaders I spoke with, thanking them for the opportunity and wishing them a successful SKO. Sales is a long game. How we show grace after a loss matters.

How to know which ads to kill or scale

1. Take every ad you're running
2. Plot it on a graph
3. Y axis = CPA
4. X axis = Spend (log)
5. Choose your target CPA
6. Define your kill CPA (typically 2-3x tCPA)
7. Draw those lines horizontally

Now you have three types of ads:

Scale = Green
→ CPA below your target line, with spend already behind them
→ Expect about 1% of your ads here. They'll drive 50% of revenue
→ Move budget 20% at a time so you don't trigger relearning

Test = Yellow
→ CPA sits between your target and kill line
→ This is most of your account, usually 65%+ of ads
→ Push more budget and watch where it lands. Drops toward target you scale, climbs past kill you cut

Kill = Red
→ CPA above your kill line with enough spend behind it
→ Enough data to be 90% confident it never hits target
→ Ideally you have zero here. If an ad got this far, you cut too slow

People tell me cold email doesn't work and then I ask how many emails they sent. 300.

Here's the threshold we actually use.

We don't call a campaign successful or unsuccessful until it has sent 1,000 emails.

If it sends 1,000 and gets one positive response, we let it run to 3,000 before we decide anything. Sometimes you just get unlucky, sometimes it is a bad week.

If it sends 1,000 and gets zero positives, we shut it off.

My full belief is that campaigns work quickly or they don't work.

You might have heard Alex Hormozi say he thought he could get outbound implemented in six months and it took a year. Fine, that is true of all of outbound. But that is the booking, the no shows, whether it is the right ICP, the sales process for a cold lead versus a warm one. Everything up to the positive response should show up fast.

So when you hit 1,000 and it is dead, before you rewrite the first line again, go check the two things that are a hard science.

Deliverability. Warmup at 100, the seed list came back clean, reply rate above 1%, the auto responder inboxes coming back over 80%, and whatever campaign you run that always works is still behaving normally.

The list. Have Claude read the whole thing and tell you whether these are actually the people you meant to email, then go look at a hundred of them yourself.

If both of those check out, stop editing the copy. Your problem is the offer, or the framing of it.

That is also why we will just run a free campaign for a company that wants to work with us. Either it works or it doesn't, and if it doesn't, you most likely need to radically change the offer.

I've advised over 100 founders on their content marketing strategy. The first thing I tell them is to write from their lived experience. Here's what I ACTUALLY mean by that:

- Start with a thing that happened, ideally in the last 7 days 

- Say when it happened and who it happened with

- Prioritise being specific and factual over impressive and interesting. e.g. writing about a client call from last Tuesday will build more trust than writing about your best ever year in business

- Share lessons, not advice. Advice is telling people what to do but a lesson is what you found out by doing it. Always write lessons.

- Frame, frame, frame. Show what most people in your market assume, THEN show what you found. 

- If anyone else in your industry could have written it, then it's not worth posting.

- Write it in your own clumsy way. The way you process thought and communicate is unique to you and that is way better than overly polished PC crap.

- If the actual writing part is blocking you from writing, voice note it. Use Wispr Flow to get it all out, then rewrite whatever comes back in your own words.

- Your niche is never too niche. There is an audience for everything. You just need to understand your TAM and reign expectations in accordingly.

None of this requires an impressive result. 

It just requires something to have happened and everyone has something happening to them, especially founders who are juggling business, health, family, relationships etc.

Hack to become a DTC CFO's best friend

Show them this data:

1. Retargeting holdout

→ Turn retargeting off for two weeks, track total revenue.
→ Incremental conversions ÷ platform-reported conversions = your incrementality rate.
→ Platform ROAS × that rate = true ROAS.
→ One brand reported 5x on retargeting. Revenue stayed flat with it off. 12.5% of those conversions were incremental, so true ROAS was 0.63x.
→ The number finance gets: discount platform retargeting revenue by 87.5%.

2. Geo holdout

→ Spend heavily in a few selected regions, hold the rest flat, measure the lift.
→ Test region revenue growth minus control region growth = your lift.
→ Extra spend in the test region ÷ incremental conversions = incremental CPA.
→ Incremental CPA ÷ platform-reported CPA = the adjustment factor for that channel.
→ Cross-check that lift against your post-purchase survey for the same window.
→ Scale only where that incremental CPA clears your break-even CPA.

3. Account-wide lift test

→ From the day a high-scaling top-of-funnel ad launches, ignore net-new launches and track aggregate ROAS of the ads already running.
→ Baseline that cohort's ROAS for the 30 days before launch. It should decline softly.
→ Cohort ROAS during the scaling window minus that baseline trend = the halo the ad is generating.
→ Example, one TOF ad: ROAS on everything else rose 45% while it ran, down 24% when paused.

4. MER and contribution margin

→ Lead the weekly report with contribution margin split across your highest value ads, sat next to revenue.
→ MER = total revenue ÷ total marketing spend.
→ Break-even ROAS = 1 ÷ contribution margin. At 60% margin that is 1.67x.
→ Report every channel against that line.

5. Survey vs last click

→ Compare your post purchase survey responses to last click UTM.
→ Survey share of a channel ÷ last click share of that channel = your adjustment multiplier.
→ If the survey shows 1.5x what Meta reports, Meta's number gets multiplied by 1.5.
→ Hand over one multiplier per channel, with the response count it came from.

6. Conversion window

→ Click attribution overvalues lower funnel by up to 250%. (Haus has shared great data here)
→ Top of funnel drives 13x more incremental acquisitions than bottom of funnel.
→ Days 20-40 is the biggest repurchase window, so a 1 day view window grades your best ads before they have done anything.
→ Same ad on a 7 day click window ÷ that ad on a 1 day view window = what your reporting window is costing top of funnel.
→ Apply a window multiplier to every top of funnel ad

What Meta ads bid strategy is best?

Full breakdown:

1. Highest Volume

→ You choose the budget. Meta spends it all.
→ Your CPA will vary to ensure the full spend.

2. Cost per Result Goal

→ You lock in a cost target.
→ A cost target rejects expensive conversions. And if cheap conversions aren't possible then you'll spend less money.
→ Set the target below your recent CPA and Meta stops bidding.
→ Meta notes: "Adherence to cost per result goal limits is not guaranteed."
→ Set it 10-20% above recent CPA and control budget by moving the cost target up and down.

3. Bid Cap

→ You lock the bid in every auction.
→ Your spend varies to whatever it takes to meet that bid.
→ This is useful when you know your exact break-even to the dollar and you're fine spending varying budgets as a result.
→ Meta notes it "does not control for the CPA that you see in reporting." You control the bid. The reported CPA is whatever the auctions produce.

How I use bidding strategies

- Highest Volume until I have a baseline CPA.
- Test a cost target after that, to steer budget and bids in and out of the right ads. Compare on performance.
- Almost never bid cap.

I've audited 200+ ABM programs

The biggest predictor of ABM success isn't your ICP, messaging, or your team. 

It’s a financial issue

The first question I always ask:

“Walk me through the math. What are we actually buying here?”

Maybe 5 had a defensible answer.

The ABM programs that get renewed are decided before launch, not after.

Here’s how to set it up correctly:

STEP 1 // BUILD YOUR COST MODEL

Total ABM investment breaks into 3 buckets:

A. Media spend
↳ LinkedIn, CTV, programmatic, direct mail
↳ Budget $150-300 per target account per month for air cover
↳ 100 accounts = $15K-$30K/month minimum

B. Tech stack
↳ Intent data, ABM platform, enrichment tools
↳ Annualize and divide by # of programs

C. People cost
↳ % of SDR, marketing, ops time dedicated to ABM
↳ Burdened salary × time allocation

Add all three = Total Program Cost

STEP 2 // MODEL YOUR EXPECTED PIPELINE

Formula:
Target Accounts × Expected Engagement Rate × Meeting Conversion × Opp Conversion × Avg Deal Size = Expected Pipeline

Example with real math:
↳ 100 accounts
↳ 25% engagement rate (25 engaged accounts)
↳ 40% meeting conversion (10 meetings)
↳ 70% opp conversion (7 opportunities)
↳ $75K avg deal size
= $525K in pipeline

STEP 3 // CALCULATE PROGRAM ROI

Pipeline ROI = Expected Pipeline / Total Program Cost

If your program costs $50K and generates $525K in pipeline:
↳ Pipeline ROI = 10.5x

But leadership cares about closed revenue, not pipeline.

Revenue ROI = (Expected Pipeline × Historical Close Rate) / Total Program Cost

↳ $525K × 30% close rate = $157.5K expected revenue
↳ $157.5K / $50K = 3.15x revenue ROI

STEP 4 // BUILD THE SENSITIVITY TABLE

This is what separates amateurs from operators.

Show leadership 3 scenarios:
↳ Conservative: 20% engagement, 25% close rate
↳ Base case: 25% engagement, 30% close rate
↳ Aggressive: 35% engagement, 35% close rate

Map each scenario to pipeline and revenue ROI.

When leadership asks "what if it doesn't work?" you already have the answer.

STEP 5 // TIE TO EXISTING BENCHMARKS

Pull your historical data:
↳ What's your current cost-per-opportunity from other channels?
↳ What's your average CAC payback?
↳ What's your LTV:CAC ratio by segment?

Show how ABM compares. If your current CPO is $8K and ABM delivers at $7.1K, that's the story.

The pitch isn't "ABM is cool." The pitch is "ABM delivers pipeline at a lower CPO than our current mix."

Programs that launch with this model don't get cut at month 9.
They get expanded.
